segment.text: 親子は、狭い部屋の壁際にぶらさがった、暗い電燈の下の卓に集まって、今夜食をしようとしてゐた。まだ本当に父も母も若かった。そして子供は漸く卓につかまって、立ってる事が出来る程の、くり〳〵と肥ってる女の子だった。

sentences.text: 親子は、狭い部屋の壁際にぶらさがった、暗い電燈の下の卓に集まって、今夜食をしようとしてゐた。
まだ本当に父も母も若かった。
そして子供は漸く卓につかまって、立ってる事が出来る程の、くり〳〵と肥ってる女の子だった。

segment.text: 男も女も、その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった。しかし男の濃い眉毛の陰のくぼんだ優しさうな瞳には、だるさうな疲れの色が見えてゐた。そして女の濃い髪のいろや、細やかな肩のあたりには、なほ打沈んだやうな深い疲れと、まどろむやうな安らかさとが見えてゐた。

segment.text: 一日が終ったのであった。その日の悲しみも苦しみも、夜の安らかさに流れやうとしてゐるのだった。そして、彼等は黙って微笑しながら、その子供のすべてに瞳を注いだ。

segment.text: 子供は、あぶなさうに立ちながら、肥えてまるく鞠のやうに短い両手で、すこしのすきまもなく、そしてあまりに早くテーブルの上のものを掻き廻さうとしてゐた。それで彼等は微笑みみながら、すべて茶碗や土瓶、アルミ鍋などを、テーブルの下に置いた。テーブルの上には、わづか子供の持つ小さなスプーンと小皿が一枚残されたばかりであった。

segment.text: 彼女は鍋から熱い炊き立ての、白い湯気が一ぱい立ち上ってる御飯をついで彼に渡した。そして彼女の若い大きな瞳も、母親らしい嬉しさにみちて子供の瞬間もぢっとしてない、小鳥のやうに愛らしい様子を見つめた。そして、たまらなささうに、この子はどうしたといふんだらう、とふと口の中に独言を云ひながら、どうにも仕方がない程可愛いといふやうな様子で、『坊や、』と強く云ったけれども、笑が顔からあふれて了って、彼女は助をかりるやうに男の顔を見た。そして三人は、すべての事を忘れてしまった様に、子供の為めに互にどうしようかといふ様に笑ひ合った。そして子供の為めに、彼等は暖かい賑かさと、其上に自然に溢れる笑ひと嬉しさを持って食事にとりかゝったのであった。また彼等は、ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に、雨風の音を耳にしない。

sentences.text: 彼女は鍋から熱い炊き立ての、白い湯気が一ぱい立ち上ってる御飯をついで彼に渡した。
そして彼女の若い大きな瞳も、母親らしい嬉しさにみちて子供の瞬間もぢっとしてない、小鳥のやうに愛らしい様子を見つめた。
そして、たまらなささうに、この子はどうしたといふんだらう、とふと口の中に独言を云ひながら、どうにも仕方がない程可愛いといふやうな様子で、『坊や、』と強く云ったけれども、笑が顔からあふれて了って、彼女は助をかりるやうに男の顔を見た。
そして三人は、すべての事を忘れてしまった様に、子供の為めに互にどうしようかといふ様に笑ひ合った。
そして子供の為めに、彼等は暖かい賑かさと、其上に自然に溢れる笑ひと嬉しさを持って食事にとりかゝったのであった。
また彼等は、ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に、雨風の音を耳にしない。

segment.text: 若い父親は、彼の赤く大きな片手を忙しくテーブルの上に拡げてゐた。そしてその眼は子供によって仕方がなく湧き出た笑を堪へながら、子供をさゝへて、その小さな赤い口に僅の食物を入れてやった。そのすきに彼は、あわたゞしく大きな口を開けた、彼は彼自身の口のなかに御飯を押し込んだ。

segment.text: 母親は、壁によって黙ってうつむきながら藍色の深い鍋に煮た牛肉と玉葱と、人参とジャガ芋とを白い皿に盛ってゐた。そしてなにか云はうとして、甘く柔かく煮たジャガ芋を口のなかに入れて、男の顔を見たが、彼女はなにかに気がついたやうに、ふと口を閉ぢて茫然と遠い所を見た。

segment.text: そして、それがあまりに永く引きつゞいた生活のやうにも思はれた。彼女はふと自分がすっかり老いてしまったかのやうに考へられた。そして静かに涙にみちた日のことや、物質の為めに脅かされ恐れてすごした日々や、病の為めに悲しみ苦しんだその日その日のことを遠い心が静かに思出してゐるのだった。けれどもいま思出してる彼女には、すべてが夢のやうであった。苦しみも悲しみもなつかしい夢のやうであった。

segment.text: それは淡暗い光りのなかに、そしてその光りのやうに物静かな三人の人たちが、より合って頭をあつめてながい物語りをしてゐるのだった。その物語りは、あまりにながく絶えることなく彼等の間につゞけられてゐるやうであった。そしてその物語りのなかには、すべて世の中の善や悪や、かなしみや苦しみ怒りもなやみも、よろこびもすべてが語られてるやうだった。けれども話す人も聞く人も、たゞ静かに安らかにぢっと微笑をつゞけてゐるばかりであって、彼等は少しも動かなかった。首をかたむけて眼を伏せながら、そして、そこにはたゞ静かななつかしみと、許しとが彼等をつつんでゐるやうに見えた。そしてまたそこには深い〳〵安らかさが彼等のすべてに表はれてゐるのであった。

hard_spots.why_hard: Potato is 凍ったかのやうに固くざくざく, 無味な、かゝはりのない冷やかな不味さ — frozen-seeming, hard, gritty/crunchy between front teeth, flavourless, cold, unconnected. Temptation is to normalise to undercooked or to symbolise poverty. Must stay oddly exact and physical; it triggers vision without dialogue.

hard_spots.kind: vision syntax and thought by circling
hard_spots.why_hard: Long durative sentences bound by soshite/keredomo, likenesses (yō), repetitions of quiet/dear/forgiveness/peace. Advances by returning, not by logic. Rationalising into tidy subordination or upgrading into heaven/death/old-age epiphany would clarify what text leaves as picture at bottom of eyes.

Child introduced as 女の子 (girl) then called 坊や (bōya, usually boy) by both parents. Fluent fix is to make child a boy. House rule: preserve as parents' fond usage; keep Bōya with note, keep she/her for narrator.
うまうまうまうま with spoon-banging while looking at mother — delight/food word, not standard delicious. Needs consistent child-voice rendering without cute ennoblement.

His rough plain (さうだなァ, 俺たち, もう少しの間だ) vs her polite feminine (ですのね, ませうね); most important thing (なにか大きな希み) is never told. Risk is making him obtuse or her articulate, or filling silence with thought-tags.

Storm goes announced → unheard in warm noisiness → heard alone by mother → whispered by husband standing still. First and last lines must stay equally bare; do not turn last line into moral or atmosphere.

Taishō domestic modernity; dimness matters for vision's dim light later. Keep literal.

motifs.english: Carry always as peace / peaceful / restfully at peace. Do not vary to calm, tranquillity, comfort. Lonely + peaceful must stay strange together.
motifs.why: Core of both supper (night's peace) and vision (deep peace, night-like rest). Network depends on same word returning in resolve.

motifs.english: Carry always as lonely (not lonesome, solitary, forlorn). Keeps worn-young ache and far-off stillness linked.
motifs.why: Potato's cold tastelessness gives her a lonely distant heart; same lonely colours the peace and the sigh. Variation would break cause.

motifs.english: Carry always as dearness (noun) / dear (adj), not nostalgia, fondness, affection. She feels tenderness for what is not yet past.
motifs.why: Moves from suffering-remembered-as-dear-dream to vision's wrapping to future change into dearness. Must be recognisable each time.

motifs.english: Carry always as forgiveness. Do not upgrade to absolution, mercy, pardon.
motifs.why: Paired with dearness every time; the vision's ethical content is only this pair plus peace. Elegant variation would invent doctrine.

motifs.english: Carry always as far / far-off / far away. Keep spatial distance for time distance (far future, far picture, far heart).
motifs.why: How interior distance is marked: looking far, picture at bottom of eyes seen through to far future. Tense-shift substitute would rationalise.

motifs.english: Carry always as smile (noun/verb), not grin, beam, laugh. Includes hohoemi, emi, warai, wariau. Laughter here is quiet overflow, not comedy.
motifs.why: Joins warm feeding noisiness to vision's unmoving smiling; same word must cover both or parallel is lost.

motifs.english: Carry looking-down vs looking-far as steady pair: gaze down / look down; gaze far / look far away. Do not psychologise to ponder, contemplate.
motifs.motif: looking down / looking far; pouring eyes
motifs.why: Body marks drift: child gets poured eyes, then downcast loneliness, then far seeing. Attributing thoughts would destroy unmarked slip.

narration.english_tense: past as default; past progressive / durative was -ing for te-ita, -tsutsu, -yō to shite iru drift (was flowing, were telling); keep dialogue present-tense force in past frame without backshifting into pluperfect explanation
narration.frame: Single-evening room interior framed by storm: announced (p1), explicitly unheard in feeding warmth (p8), heard alone by mother with returning picture (p19), whispered standing still by husband after child asleep (p38). No chapter break; vision interrupts supper without announcement and returns without report.
narration.narrator: heterodiegetic, soft and close, mostly with mother but starting as joint parental view; slips without announcement from room to inner seeing and back; dropped subjects and unmarked whose-eyes shifts are part of drift — repair only what English cannot carry, never add 'she thought' or 'in her mind's eye'
narration.tense_habits: Historical-kana Taishō literary past interwoven with durative -te ita / -tsutsu aru / -yō to suru; likenesses (yō ni, ka no yō ni) and soshite/keredomo chains stretch time; short colloquial dialogue in present plain/polite cuts against them
timeline: evening present: storm outside, narrow room, supper begins (p1-p9)
potato mouthful detaches mother; recollection of 3-year married poverty/illness/fear as lifetime and old age, felt as dear dream (p10-p14)
far-off picture of three telling endless story in dim light; understanding that past will change into dearness/forgiveness before night-like rest (p15-p17)
return to table with lonely sigh and glance; husband twice asks why silent; outside storm heard alone (p18-p19)
circling resolve without reporting vision: only three years passed, large hope she cannot name, child will walk, only a little longer (p20-p34)
clear table, sleep, early rise; child asleep at breast; quiet; whispered storm to close (p35-p38)

body.say: Time dilates through a bad mouthful, not through talk: keep supper exact, vision dim and circling, repetition steady, and ending modest — clear, sleep, rise early.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Casual: 1–2 notes (Bōya-for-girl, umma-umma); Curious: + dobin/indigo pot, storm frame, dearness/forgiveness choice; Student: + historical kana/ruby, aluminium, durative syntax, vision non-resolution. Never note what context supplies.
style_sheet.author_voice: Soft, drifting, durative; long soshite/keredomo sentences full of as-if likenesses, then short bangs of child noise and brief dialogue. Neither lyrical-poor nor squalid; young-and-already-worn held together. English must be signable prose that resists tidying: no rationalised subordination, no varied synonyms for network words, no explained epiphany.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: No surnames or honorifics in text; do not invent. Keep Bōya capitalised as address; keep narrator she/her for mother, she/her for girl child. Name order n/a.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: All views: Bōya, umma-umma (first use glossed). Curious/Student also keep dobin with gloss. Otherwise render, do not costume with san/chan or unglossed period terms.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese 『』 dialogue to English double quotes; inner 独言 (monologue aloud/in mouth) stays as quoted or unquoted speech per passage flow, not italicised thought; child's babble in quotes with exclamation as given.
style_sheet.register: Modern plain literary English for narration, no Taishō costume or archaism; dialogue split — his plain rough, her quiet polite-formal — without dialect caricature; baby noise vivid and physical
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Do not carry ruby as parentheses: 卓《テーブル》 → table; 怜悧《れいり》 → shrewd; 微笑《ほゝゑみ》 → smile; 茫然《ぼんやり》 → vaguely/vacantly. No italics for emphasis or thought; italics only for first-use kept Japanese items (Bōya, umma-umma, dobin) where house style requires.
standing_rules: Do not correct girl to boy: girl child addressed as Bōya throughout.
Keep potato adjectives exact and unconnected: frozen-seeming, hard, gritty, flavourless, cold — no diagnosis.
Keep network words invariant: peace/rest, lonely, dearness, forgiveness, far, smile, silent, gaze down/far.
Do not add attributions (she thought, she saw in her mind) where Japanese lets picture be there.
Keep storm first/last lines equally bare; do not moralise ending beyond clear table, sleep, rise early.
Scope: all views, all paragraphs; passage wins over bible — flag conflict plainly.

Child introduced as 女の子 (girl) then called 坊や (bōya, usually boy) by both parents. Fluent fix is to make child a boy. House rule: preserve as parents' fond usage; keep Bōya with note, keep she/her for narrator.

style_sheet.author_voice: Soft, drifting, durative; long soshite/keredomo sentences full of as-if likenesses, then short bangs of child noise and brief dialogue. Neither lyrical-poor nor squalid; young-and-already-worn held together. English must be signable prose that resists tidying: no rationalised subordination, no varied synonyms for network words, no explained epiphany.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: No surnames or honorifics in text; do not invent. Keep Bōya capitalised as address; keep narrator she/her for mother, she/her for girl child. Name order n/a.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: All views: Bōya, umma-umma (first use glossed). Curious/Student also keep dobin with gloss. Otherwise render, do not costume with san/chan or unglossed period terms.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese 『』 dialogue to English double quotes; inner 独言 (monologue aloud/in mouth) stays as quoted or unquoted speech per passage flow, not italicised thought; child's babble in quotes with exclamation as given.
style_sheet.register: Modern plain literary English for narration, no Taishō costume or archaism; dialogue split — his plain rough, her quiet polite-formal — without dialect caricature; baby noise vivid and physical
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Do not carry ruby as parentheses: 卓《テーブル》 → table; 怜悧《れいり》 → shrewd; 微笑《ほゝゑみ》 → smile; 茫然《ぼんやり》 → vaguely/vacantly. No italics for emphasis or thought; italics only for first-use kept Japanese items (Bōya, umma-umma, dobin) where house style requires.
standing_rules: Do not correct girl to boy: girl child addressed as Bōya throughout.
Keep potato adjectives exact and unconnected: frozen-seeming, hard, gritty, flavourless, cold — no diagnosis.
Keep network words invariant: peace/rest, lonely, dearness, forgiveness, far, smile, silent, gaze down/far.
Do not add attributions (she thought, she saw in her mind) where Japanese lets picture be there.
Keep storm first/last lines equally bare; do not moralise ending beyond clear table, sleep, rise early.
Scope: all views, all paragraphs; passage wins over bible — flag conflict plainly.

hard_spots.why_hard: Potato is 凍ったかのやうに固くざくざく, 無味な、かゝはりのない冷やかな不味さ — frozen-seeming, hard, gritty/crunchy between front teeth, flavourless, cold, unconnected. Temptation is to normalise to undercooked or to symbolise poverty. Must stay oddly exact and physical; it triggers vision without dialogue.

hard_spots.kind: vision syntax and thought by circling
hard_spots.why_hard: Long durative sentences bound by soshite/keredomo, likenesses (yō), repetitions of quiet/dear/forgiveness/peace. Advances by returning, not by logic. Rationalising into tidy subordination or upgrading into heaven/death/old-age epiphany would clarify what text leaves as picture at bottom of eyes.

Child introduced as 女の子 (girl) then called 坊や (bōya, usually boy) by both parents. Fluent fix is to make child a boy. House rule: preserve as parents' fond usage; keep Bōya with note, keep she/her for narrator.
うまうまうまうま with spoon-banging while looking at mother — delight/food word, not standard delicious. Needs consistent child-voice rendering without cute ennoblement.

His rough plain (さうだなァ, 俺たち, もう少しの間だ) vs her polite feminine (ですのね, ませうね); most important thing (なにか大きな希み) is never told. Risk is making him obtuse or her articulate, or filling silence with thought-tags.

Storm goes announced → unheard in warm noisiness → heard alone by mother → whispered by husband standing still. First and last lines must stay equally bare; do not turn last line into moral or atmosphere.

motifs.english: Carry always as peace / peaceful / restfully at peace. Do not vary to calm, tranquillity, comfort. Lonely + peaceful must stay strange together.
motifs.why: Core of both supper (night's peace) and vision (deep peace, night-like rest). Network depends on same word returning in resolve.

motifs.english: Carry always as lonely (not lonesome, solitary, forlorn). Keeps worn-young ache and far-off stillness linked.
motifs.why: Potato's cold tastelessness gives her a lonely distant heart; same lonely colours the peace and the sigh. Variation would break cause.

motifs.english: Carry always as dearness (noun) / dear (adj), not nostalgia, fondness, affection. She feels tenderness for what is not yet past.
motifs.why: Moves from suffering-remembered-as-dear-dream to vision's wrapping to future change into dearness. Must be recognisable each time.

motifs.english: Carry always as forgiveness. Do not upgrade to absolution, mercy, pardon.
motifs.why: Paired with dearness every time; the vision's ethical content is only this pair plus peace. Elegant variation would invent doctrine.

motifs.english: Carry always as far / far-off / far away. Keep spatial distance for time distance (far future, far picture, far heart).
motifs.why: How interior distance is marked: looking far, picture at bottom of eyes seen through to far future. Tense-shift substitute would rationalise.

motifs.english: Carry always as smile (noun/verb), not grin, beam, laugh. Includes hohoemi, emi, warai, wariau. Laughter here is quiet overflow, not comedy.
motifs.why: Joins warm feeding noisiness to vision's unmoving smiling; same word must cover both or parallel is lost.

motifs.english: Carry looking-down vs looking-far as steady pair: gaze down / look down; gaze far / look far away. Do not psychologise to ponder, contemplate.
motifs.motif: looking down / looking far; pouring eyes
motifs.why: Body marks drift: child gets poured eyes, then downcast loneliness, then far seeing. Attributing thoughts would destroy unmarked slip.

head.reason: Option 1 names a testable crux — the tasteless potato opening the still, unsettled vision of p11–p20, and its return to the plain resumed supper of the frame — where Option 0, in the form before the desk, states nothing that could be said either to coincide with or differ from it. Option 1 also follows the reading: it protects the vision's vagueness and repeated abstract words, and keeps the affirmation embodied in the tired domestic close rather than clarified into consolation.
head.say: Pick: Option 1, the crux check (Wonder). Option 0 as received contains no crux to compare — only the truncated heading 'For the English:' — so the two do not name the same thing in different words, and there is nothing in Option 0 the desk could responsibly choose as written. Option 1 does the work the choice is for: it locates the story's turn in the hard, tasteless potato of p11, holds the p16–p20 vision unsettled between death, old age and exhausted trance, ties the revaluation of the three years (p13 against p14, p22, p27) to that vision, and binds the whole to the exact frame of storm heard, unheard and named again (p8, p19, p38). Query to the owner of Option 0: supply the missing text if the truncation was unintended. House log: The desk adopts Option 1 as the crux for 『晩餐』 and asks that Option 0's missing crux be supplied for the record.

crux.for_the_english: Do not clarify the vision into old age, heaven, a memory, or a symbol with named participants. Keep its vagueness, its level abstract vocabulary, and its repetitions — 安らかさ, なつかしみ/懐しみ, 許し, 静か — returning as the same English words, not elegant synonyms. Let tense and distance drift as hers does; rationalising the syntax into a explained consolation would make the consolation cheaper and more certain than it is.
crux.point: The tasteless potato opens a still, distant vision (p11–p20) in which an only-three-years marriage feels like a whole life, and the whole of life is imagined from beyond itself — three quiet figures telling an endless story in which good, evil, sorrow, anger and joy remain, but are wrapped in なつかしみ, 許し and 安らかさ, on the threshold of a night-like eternal rest. Whether this is death, extreme old age, or a trance of exhaustion is never settled, and that unsettledness is the story.
crux.why: The turn is deliberately slight — a hard, tasteless mouthful, 凍ったかのやうに固くざくざく — and then her heart slips 遠く, repeatedly, until time itself revalues: what oppressed her as endless (p13) becomes, on return, the same fact as hope, わづかに…三年ばかり (p14) and まだ三年しか (p22, p27).

crux.for_the_english: Keep the diction plain, tired and repetitive rather than lyrical in a polished way, and keep the mirrored phrasing of the closing exchanges so the reader hears the same three years first as a lifetime of suffering and then as only three years, with work and tomorrow still ahead. Do not sentimentalise the child into a 'message': the hope has to stay embodied — spoon banging, feeding, nursing, clearing up, the storm heard again at the end (p38) — not stated as uplift.
crux.point: The return from the vision is not an argument but a resumed supper: the second crux is that the story's affirmation is made by the same tired young bodies, cheap food and storm it began with, not by escaping them.
crux.why: The frame is exact: the storm unheard in absorption (p8), heard inside the vision (p19), and named last, 嵐だな (p38); the table cleared, the child asleep at the breast, 起きよう for tomorrow (p36). If the English ennobles the poverty or separates the visionary middle from this domestic plainness, she becomes a poetess commenting on life instead of a exhausted mother whose distance is briefly real and then set down.

second.say:
Crux check — 晩餐 (Shiraki Shizu)

**1. The vision must stay unresolved.** The tasteless potato (p11) slips the mother into a distant stillness (p15–p20) where three years of marriage feel like a lifetime, and life itself is seen from beyond its end — three quiet figures, an endless story containing good and evil, sorrow and joy, all held in なつかしみ, 許し and 安らかさ before a night-like rest. Whether this is death, old age, or exhaustion is never settled; settling it would rewrite the story. *For the English:* do not gloss the vision as heaven, memory, or symbol; keep its vagueness, and repeat the same plain words for 安らかさ／なつかしみ／許し each time rather than varying them elegantly. Let tense and distance drift as hers do.

**2. The hope is the same fact read again, inside the same supper.** What crushes her as an endless life (p13) returns, unchanged, as わづかに三年ばかり (p14) and まだ三年しか (p22, p27) — and becomes grounds for もう少しの間だ, 働きませうね, and rising early tomorrow (p34–p36), framed by the storm unheard (p8), heard (p19), and named again at the close (p38). *For the English:* keep the mirrored phrasing so the reversal is heard, keep the diction plain and repetitive rather than polished, and never sentimentalise the child into a message — the affirmation must stay embodied in spoon-banging, feeding, nursing and clearing the table.

**Confidence:** High on both, from the text's own repetitions and frame. What would change my mind: house evidence from elsewhere in Shizu's work that the p16 figures are a specific doctrinal or biographical reference — then the vision should be pinned to that, not left open.

crux.for_the_english: Do not clarify the vision into old age, heaven, a memory, or a symbol with named participants. Keep its vagueness, its level abstract vocabulary, and its repetitions — 安らかさ, なつかしみ/懐しみ, 許し, 静か — returning as the same English words, not elegant synonyms. Let tense and distance drift as hers does; rationalising the syntax into a explained consolation would make the consolation cheaper and more certain than it is.
crux.point: The tasteless potato opens a still, distant vision (p11–p20) in which an only-three-years marriage feels like a whole life, and the whole of life is imagined from beyond itself — three quiet figures telling an endless story in which good, evil, sorrow, anger and joy remain, but are wrapped in なつかしみ, 許し and 安らかさ, on the threshold of a night-like eternal rest. Whether this is death, extreme old age, or a trance of exhaustion is never settled, and that unsettledness is the story.
crux.why: The turn is deliberately slight — a hard, tasteless mouthful, 凍ったかのやうに固くざくざく — and then her heart slips 遠く, repeatedly, until time itself revalues: what oppressed her as endless (p13) becomes, on return, the same fact as hope, わづかに…三年ばかり (p14) and まだ三年しか (p22, p27).

crux.for_the_english: Keep the diction plain, tired and repetitive rather than lyrical in a polished way, and keep the mirrored phrasing of the closing exchanges so the reader hears the same three years first as a lifetime of suffering and then as only three years, with work and tomorrow still ahead. Do not sentimentalise the child into a 'message': the hope has to stay embodied — spoon banging, feeding, nursing, clearing up, the storm heard again at the end (p38) — not stated as uplift.
crux.point: The return from the vision is not an argument but a resumed supper: the second crux is that the story's affirmation is made by the same tired young bodies, cheap food and storm it began with, not by escaping them.
crux.why: The frame is exact: the storm unheard in absorption (p8), heard inside the vision (p19), and named last, 嵐だな (p38); the table cleared, the child asleep at the breast, 起きよう for tomorrow (p36). If the English ennobles the poverty or separates the visionary middle from this domestic plainness, she becomes a poetess commenting on life instead of a exhausted mother whose distance is briefly real and then set down.

body.reading:
The crux is a dilation of time inside an otherwise unremarkable supper, and the translation stands or falls on not explaining it. A young, poor couple are eating with their baby in a narrow room while a storm goes on outside. The mother puts a softly cooked potato in her mouth and finds it hard, gritty, as if frozen, and very bad. Nothing is made of this in dialogue — no complaint, no apology for the cooking — but the tasteless, cold mouthful detaches her. Fatigue, the sadnesses of their married poverty, illness and fear over money, suddenly feel as if they have lasted a lifetime and as if she has grown old; in the same movement she sees, far off and dim, three quiet figures with their heads together telling one endless story in which everything in the world — good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, worry, joy — is being told, while the tellers only smile, unmoving, wrapped in a quiet dearness and forgiveness and a deep peace. She understands, in her own circling terms, that a day will come when everything past will have changed into that dearness and forgiveness, before an eternal, night-like rest. Then the arithmetic returns: it has, in fact, been only three years since the marriage. The rest of the story is her carrying that vision back into the room — twice asked by her husband why she is silent, twice unable to say it — and turning it, without ever reporting it, into a resolve that they will work, that the child will walk, that there is only a little longer to bear. If English makes this a stated epiphany, a vision of heaven, a premonition of death, or a lesson about poverty, it has clarified what Shiraki leaves as a picture seen at the bottom of the eyes; if it makes it merely a tired daydream, it has flattened the one event the story has.

Keep the mechanism plain and physical. The potato passage must stay oddly exact — frozen-seeming, gritty between the front teeth, flavourless, cold, unconnected — because the vision grows out of that sensory wrongness and out of accumulated tiredness, not out of any remark or symbol offered by the narrator. The mother puts a softly cooked potato in her mouth and finds it hard, gritty, as if frozen, and very bad. Nothing is made of this in dialogue — no complaint, no apology for the cooking — but the tasteless, cold mouthful detaches her. Fatigue, the sadnesses of their married poverty, illness and fear over money, suddenly feel as if they have lasted a lifetime and as if she has grown old; in the same movement she sees, far off and dim, three quiet figures with their heads together telling one endless story in which everything in the world — good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, worry, joy — is being told, while the tellers only smile, unmoving, wrapped in a quiet dearness and forgiveness and a deep peace. She understands, in her own circling terms, that a day will come when everything past will have changed into that dearness and forgiveness, before an eternal, night-like rest. Then the arithmetic returns: it has, in fact, been only three years since the marriage. The rest of the story is her carrying that vision back into the room — twice asked by her husband why she is silent, twice unable to say it — and turning it, without ever reporting it, into a resolve that they will work, that the child will walk, that there is only a little longer to bear. If English makes this a stated epiphany, a vision of heaven, a premonition of death, or a lesson about poverty, it has clarified what Shiraki leaves as a picture seen at the bottom of the eyes; if it makes it merely a tired daydream, it has flattened the one event the story has.

Keep the mechanism plain and physical. The potato passage must stay oddly exact — frozen-seeming, gritty between the front teeth, flavourless, cold, unconnected — because the vision grows out of that sensory wrongness and out of accumulated tiredness, not out of any remark or symbol offered by the narrator. Likewise keep the domestic business exact and unembellished: bowls and the earthen bottle and the aluminium pot cleared under the table out of the baby's reach, the spoon and small plate left, rice steaming from the pot, beef and onion and carrot and potato served from a deep indigo pot, the child banged and fed and finally asleep at the breast. The vision is credible only because the supper is not. Do not let the prose ennoble either side: no lyrical poverty, no squalor either. They are young — the text insists neither face has a wrinkle yet — and already worn, his tiredness in the hollowed, gentle eyes under thick brows, hers in the dark hair and slight shoulders. That double fact, young and exhausted, is what makes her feeling of having aged, and of a life already very long, land.

The sound is long, drifting, durative sentences bound by *soshite* and *keredomo*, full of likenesses — as if a dream, as if a picture, as if far away — and then, against them, short exchanges of dialogue and the child's noise. English will want to rationalise the long sentences into tidy subordination and to vary the words they repeat; resist both. The repetition is the thought. *Shizuka*, *yasuraka*, *samishii/sabishii*, *natsukashii*, *yurushi*, *tooii*, smiling, looking down, looking far away: this small network has to recur in the same English words, so that when "dearness and forgiveness" returns in her silent resolve the reader feels the vision still operating rather than a new sentiment being introduced. In particular do not upgrade *natsukashimi* into full "nostalgia" every time if it makes it sound like a concept; she is feeling a tenderness toward what has not yet even become past. Keep "peace/rest" similarly steady for the *yasuraka-* family, and let the strangeness of feeling it as lonely — a lonely peace, a lonely sigh — survive.

Register is Taishō literary prose in historical kana, but it is not quaint, and the English should not wear period costume. The narration is soft and close, moving without announcement from the room into the mother's inner seeing and back; dropped subjects and unmarked shifts of whose eyes we are through are part of that drift, so repair only what English genuinely cannot carry, and never add attributions ("she thought to herself", "in her mind's eye") where the Japanese simply lets the picture be there. A young, poor couple are eating with their baby in a narrow room while a storm goes on outside. The mother puts a softly cooked potato in her mouth and finds it hard, gritty, as if frozen, and very bad. Fatigue, the sadnesses of their married poverty, illness and fear over money, suddenly feel as if they have lasted a lifetime and as if she has grown old; in the same movement she sees, far off and dim, three quiet figures with their heads together telling one endless story in which everything in the world — good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, worry, joy — is being told, while the tellers only smile, unmoving, wrapped in a quiet dearness and forgiveness and a deep peace. She understands, in her own circling terms, that a day will come when everything past will have changed into that dearness and forgiveness, before an eternal, night-like rest. Then the arithmetic returns: it has, in fact, been only three years since the marriage. They are young — the text insists neither face has a wrinkle yet — and already worn, his tiredness in the hollowed, gentle eyes under thick brows, hers in the dark hair and slight shoulders. In particular do not upgrade *natsukashimi* into full "nostalgia" every time if it makes it sound like a concept; she is feeling a tenderness toward what has not yet even become past. Keep "peace/rest" similarly steady for the *yasuraka-* family, and let the strangeness of feeling it as lonely — a lonely peace, a lonely sigh — survive.

- Who are the three figures in the vision — the couple and their grown child, the couple grown old with someone else, or no identifiable persons at all? term.reading: あいいろのふかいなべ
term.student: deep indigo pot [ai-iro no fukai nabe]
term.rationale: 藍色の深い鍋 beef/onion/carrot/potato is served from; colour kept as indigo/blue, not aestheticised.
Period poverty marker; keep metal plain, do not ennoble or squalidify.
Frame word. Same plain English everywhere so unheard / heard-inwardly / spoken progression is visible.

term.student: Bōya [坊や — fond address for a small child, here used to a girl]
term.rationale: Parents' fond address to girl child; capitalised kept Japanese in all views with one note, never he/him correction. Proposed, house to approve.

term.student: dim electric light [dentō, historical kana 電燈]
term.rationale: Taishō domestic modernity; dimness matters for vision's dim light later. Keep literal.

term.student: dobin [土瓶, earthenware bottle for tea]
term.rationale: 土瓶 cleared under table out of reach. Casual glosses function; Curious/Student keep dobin with note. Proposed, house to approve.
甘く柔かく煮たはずが frozen-hard, gritty, tasteless-cold. Keep potato (not potatoe/archaic), adjectives exact per hard spot.
Ruby 卓《テーブル》 marks a Western-style table in a narrow room; once established as table, keep table, not desk.
炊き立て白い湯気 domestic exactness that makes vision credible; keep steam and white.
Baby food-joy babble while banging spoon. Keep babble with hyphenation steady, gloss once as yum-yum/food.

revision.english: Outside the door, darkened by now, there was the sound of hard wind and rain — a {t:arashi}.

The parents had gathered around the {t:table} under the dim {t:dento} hanging by the wall of the narrow room, about to take their supper. Father and mother were both still truly young. And the child was a girl, plump and round, just able to stand holding on to the {t:table}.
notes: p2-s3 fixes the child as a girl; Bōya later is kept as the parents' fond address, not a change of sex.

revision.english: Neither the man nor the woman had yet a single wrinkle in the face. But in the hollowed, gentle-looking eyes in the shadow of the man's thick brows there showed a languid colour of tiredness. And in the dark colour of the woman's hair and about her slight shoulders there showed a still more sunken deep tiredness, and a drowsy-like peace.
notes: Keeps peace steady for the yasuraka- family; keeps young-and-already-worn together without ennobling.

revision.english: The day had ended. The sadness and suffering of that day were about to flow into the peace of the night. And silent, smiling, they poured their eyes upon all that was the child.
notes: Keeps silent/smile/peace invariant; pours eyes rather than psychologising the gaze.

revision.english: The child, standing precariously, with fat, round, ball-like short hands, was about to sweep at the things on the {t:table}, without leaving a moment's gap, and far too fast. So, smiling, they put everything — bowls and {t:dobin} and {t:alumi-nabe} and the rest — under the {t:table}. On top of the {t:table} there was left only the small spoon the child held and a single small plate.
notes: Clears the supper things under the table out of reach, as written; leaves spoon and plate as the only things above.

revision.english: But the child, letting out a noisy shout full of small joy, banged spoon and plate down upon the {t:table}.

"Won't listen, will you." The young father, gazing steadily at the small round arms and at the child's long-lashed, darkish eyes moving nimbly and shrewdly without a moment's pause, as if at a loss what to do, at last with a face full of smile pinched the round jutting cheek lightly with his fingers, and taking a large bowl from under the {t:table} as if groping for it, put it into her hands.
notes: 彼女の手 is left as 'her hands' to preserve the ambiguity: narrator's 彼女 is otherwise the mother, but here the bowl after the cheek-pinch could go to the girl child's hands. Passage, not bible, should settle it.
怜悧 with ruby れいり rendered as 'shrewdly' per style sheet; 微笑 with ruby ほゝゑみ kept in smile network as 'smile'.

revision.english: She served the {t:takitate-gohan} from the pot, hot, with white steam rising thick, and handed it to him. And her young large eyes too, full of a mother's gladness, gazed at the child who was not still for an instant, lovely like a small bird. And as if she could not bear it, muttering in her mouth, "Whatever is to be done with this child," as if she found her adorable beyond all help, she said firmly, "{t:boya}," but the smile overflowed from her face, and as if to borrow help she looked at the man's face. And the three, as if having forgotten everything, smiled together as if wondering what each should do for the child. And for the child they set about their meal with a warm bustle and with the smile and gladness overflowing of itself on top of it. And in the cluttering noisiness they did not hear the sound of the wind and rain.
notes: 口のうちに独言 kept as half-aloud muttering in quoted speech, not italicised thought, per style sheet.
雨風の音 here is not given as {t:arashi}; kept as 'wind and rain' to preserve the frame progression from unheard noise to named storm.

revision.english: The young father kept his red, large hand spread busily over the {t:table}. And his eyes holding back the smile that welled up helplessly because of the child, he steadied the child and put a little food into that small red mouth. In the gap he opened a large mouth hastily, and pushed rice into his own mouth.
notes: 彼 / 彼自身 repetition kept as 'he / his own mouth,' both clearly the father steadying the child; 笑 kept in smile network.

revision.english: The mother, leaning against the wall, silent and gazing down, was serving the beef and onion, and carrot and {t:jagaimo}, simmered in the {t:aiiro-nabe}, onto a white plate. And as if about to say something, she put a {t:jagaimo} simmered sweet and soft into her mouth and looked at the man's face, but as if noticing something, she shut her mouth and gazed vaguely at a far place.
notes: kabe ni yotte taken as leaning against the wall, not sitting by the wall; posture carries the drift into downcast stillness.
bonyari for bozen kept as vaguely to match voice reference and bible, not vacantly.

revision.english: The {t:jagaimo} in her mouth was hard and gritty, as if frozen, and very bad. As if taken by surprise, she silently chewed it again with her front teeth, but her heart had already gazed down, lonely.
notes: kept potato adjectives exact and unconnected per hard spot: hard and gritty as if frozen, very bad; no diagnosis of undercooking.
kokoro ga sabishiku utsumuite: kept lonely with gaze down to hold network pair, against fluent urge to psychologize as saddened.

revision.english: She remembered the suffering and sadness and tiredness of her days. And the flavourless, unconnected, cold badness of the {t:jagaimo} gave her a quiet, lonely, far-removed heart. She pictured the poor, sorrow-filled, real life after marriage.
notes: mumyona, kakawari no nai, tsumetai mazusa kept as three unlinked adjectives — flavourless, unconnected, cold — per bible; not smoothed into one tastelessness.
far-removed heart keeps tooi/tooku as spatial distance for interior state.

revision.english: And it seemed, too, like a life drawn out very long. She felt suddenly as if she herself had quite grown old. And of quietly tear-filled days, and of days spent threatened and afraid over material things, and of each day grieved and suffered through illness, her far heart was quietly remembering. But to her remembering now, everything was like a dream. Suffering and sadness too were like a dear dream.
notes: natsukashii yume kept as dear dream per network, not nostalgic dream; tenderness toward what is not yet past.
long soshite/keredomo circling kept as paratactic And-sentences; far heart repeated, not varied.

revision.english: And when she thought, it was no more than barely three years of life after marriage.
notes: single bare arithmetic sentence kept short against the long drift either side; no expansion.

revision.english: Before she knew, as if caught by something, she was gazing vaguely far away. Her quiet heart was, before she knew, seeing a picture as if a phantom.
notes: itsutonaku twice kept as before she knew to keep durative vagueness, not tidied to suddenly.
maboroshi no you na e kept as picture as if a phantom, not vision or apparition, to avoid clarifying into heaven/death; no added she thought / in her mind.

revision.english: It was in a faintly dim light, and, quiet like that light, three people drawing close with their heads together were telling a long story. That story seemed to go on and on between them without ever breaking. And within that story it seemed that everything in the world was being told — good and evil, sorrow and suffering and anger and worry, joy, everything. But teller and listener alike only went on smiling, quietly and peacefully and motionlessly, and they did not move at all. fork.question: What does a translation of this text stand or fall on?

options.author: crux-check (Wonder)
options.case:
- The tasteless potato opens a still, distant vision (p11–p20) in which an only-three-years marriage feels like a whole life, and the whole of life is imagined from beyond itself — three quiet figures telling an endless story in which good, evil, sorrow, anger and joy remain, but are wrapped in なつかしみ, 許し and 安らかさ, on the threshold of a night-like eternal rest. Whether this is death, extreme old age, or a trance of exhaustion is never settled, and that unsettledness is the story. The turn is deliberately slight — a hard, tasteless mouthful, 凍ったかのやうに固くざくざく — and then her heart slips 遠く, repeatedly, until time itself revalues: what oppressed her as endless (p13) becomes, on return, the same fact as hope, わづかに…三年ばかり (p14) and まだ三年しか (p22, p27). For the English: Do not clarify the vision into old age, heaven, a memory, or a symbol with named participants. Keep its vagueness, its level abstract vocabulary, and its repetitions — 安らかさ, なつかしみ/懐しみ, 許し, 静か — returning as the same English words, not elegant synonyms. Let tense and distance drift as hers does; rationalising the syntax into a explained consolation would make the consolation cheaper and more certain than it is.
- The return from the vision is not an argument but a resumed supper: the second crux is that the story's affirmation is made by the same tired young bodies, cheap food and storm it began with, not by escaping them. The frame is exact: the storm unheard in absorption (p8), heard inside the vision (p19), and named last, 嵐だな (p38); the table cleared, the child asleep at the breast, 起きよう for tomorrow (p36). If the English ennobles the poverty or separates the visionary middle from this domestic plainness, she becomes a poetess commenting on life instead of a exhausted mother whose distance is briefly real and then set down. For the English: Keep the diction plain, tired and repetitive rather than lyrical in a polished way, and keep the mirrored phrasing of the closing exchanges so the reader hears the same three years first as a lifetime of suffering and then as only three years, with work and tomorrow still ahead. Do not sentimentalise the child into a 'message': the hope has to stay embodied — spoon banging, feeding, nursing, clearing up, the storm heard again at the end (p38) — not stated as uplift.

fork.head_reason: Option 1 names a testable crux — the tasteless potato opening the still, unsettled vision of p11–p20, and its return to the plain resumed supper of the frame — where Option 0, in the form before the desk, states nothing that could be said either to coincide with or differ from it. Option 1 also follows the reading: it protects the vision's vagueness and repeated abstract words, and keeps the affirmation embodied in the tired domestic close rather than clarified into consolation.

payload.say:
The crux is a dilation of time inside an otherwise unremarkable supper, and the translation stands or falls on not explaining it. A young, poor couple are eating with their baby in a narrow room while a storm goes on outside. The mother puts a softly cooked potato in her mouth and finds it hard, gritty, as if frozen, and very bad. Nothing is made of this in dialogue — no complaint, no apology for the cooking — but the tasteless, cold mouthful detaches her. Fatigue, the sadnesses of their married poverty, illness and fear over money, suddenly feel as if they have lasted a lifetime and as if she has grown old; in the same movement she sees, far off and dim, three quiet figures with their heads together telling one endless story in which everything in the world — good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, worry, joy — is being told, while the tellers only smile, unmoving, wrapped in a quiet dearness and forgiveness and a deep peace. She understands, in her own circling terms, that a day will come when everything past will have changed into that dearness and forgiveness, before an eternal, night-like rest. Then the arithmetic returns: it has, in fact, been only three years since the marriage. The rest of the story is her carrying that vision back into the room — twice asked by her husband why she is silent, twice unable to say it — and turning it, without ever reporting it, into a resolve that they will work, that the child will walk, that there is only a little longer to bear. If English makes this a stated epiphany, a vision of heaven, a premonition of death, or a lesson about poverty, it has clarified what Shiraki leaves as a picture seen at the bottom of the eyes; if it makes it merely a tired daydream, it has flattened the one event the story has.

Keep the mechanism plain and physical. The potato passage must stay oddly exact — frozen-seeming, gritty between the front teeth, flavourless, cold, unconnected — because the vision grows out of that sensory wrongness and out of accumulated tiredness, not out of any remark or symbol offered by the narrator. Likewise keep the domestic business exact and unembellished: bowls and the earthen bottle and the aluminium pot cleared under the table out of the baby's reach, the spoon and small plate left, rice steaming from the pot, beef and onion and carrot and potato served from a deep indigo pot, the child banged and fed and finally asleep at the breast. The vision is credible only because the supper is not. Do not let the prose ennoble either side: no lyrical poverty, no squalor either. They are young — the text insists neither face has a wrinkle yet — and already worn, his tiredness in the hollowed, gentle eyes under thick brows, hers in the dark hair and slight shoulders. That double fact, young and exhausted, is what makes her feeling of having aged, and of a life already very long, land.

The sound is long, drifting, durative sentences bound by *soshite* and *keredomo*, full of likenesses — as if a dream, as if a picture, as if far away — and then, against them, short exchanges of dialogue and the child's noise. English will want to rationalise the long sentences into tidy subordination and to vary the words they repeat; resist both. The repetition is the thought. *Shizuka*, *yasuraka*, *samishii/sabishii*, *natsukashii*, *yurushi*, *tooii*, smiling, looking down, looking far away: this small network has to recur in the same English words, so that when "dearness and forgiveness" returns in her silent resolve the reader feels the vision still operating rather than a new sentiment being introduced. In particular do not upgrade *natsukashimi* into full "nostalgia" every time if it makes it sound like a concept; she is feeling a tenderness toward what has not yet even become past. Keep "peace/rest" similarly steady for the *yasuraka-* family, and let the strangeness of feeling it as lonely — a lonely peace, a lonely sigh — survive.

Register is Taishō literary prose in historical kana, but it is not quaint, and the English should not wear period costume. The narration is soft and close, moving without announcement from the room into the mother's inner seeing and back; dropped subjects and unmarked shifts of whose eyes we are through are part of that drift, so repair only what English genuinely cannot carry, and never add attributions ("she thought to herself", "in her mind's eye") where the Japanese simply lets the picture be there. The dialogue is the opposite register: brief, colloquial, his rougher *sō da nā*, *ore-tachi*, her polite feminine forms and her careful *watashitachi wa hatarakimashō ne*. Give her speech a quiet formality and his a plainer roughness without caricature, and keep how little is actually said: he asks twice why she is silent, she answers only that it has really been barely three years, and the most important thing she has to tell him — something large she herself does not understand — is never told. Do not make him obtuse for not understanding, nor her articulate.

Note the frame and do not break it. The storm is announced in the first line, forgotten in the warm noisiness of feeding the child (the text says outright that they do not hear it), heard again by the mother alone at the moment the vision returns, and finally named by the husband, standing still and whispering, after the child is asleep and the room has gone quiet. That progression — unheard, heard inwardly, spoken — is the story's only plot, and the last line must stay as bare as the first. The child is its counterweight throughout: fat, round, precariously standing, banging spoon and plate, crying *umamma* with delight, impossible to keep still for an instant. Keep her vivid and noisy rather than adorable in a generalised way; her present-tense liveliness is what the mother's far-off stillness is seen across, and what the resolve at the end is for. Watch also the small, easy-to-smooth contradiction that the baby is introduced as a girl and then addressed as *bōya*: preserve the address as the parents' fond usage rather than silently correcting the child into a boy.

The likeliest fluent failures, in Berman's terms, are clarification of the vision into old age, death or heaven; destruction of the repeated-word network by elegant variation; rationalisation of the circling sentences in paragraphs 16–20, which think by returning rather than advancing; and ennoblement of the ending into inspiration. The ending is modest: clear the table, sleep, get up early tomorrow. Let it be.

Open questions:
- Who are the three figures in the vision — the couple and their grown child, the couple grown old with someone else, or no identifiable persons at all? The text says only "three people" in dim light; any identification the English adds, even by pronoun or age, settles what Shiraki leaves unsettled, and the choice will colour whether the vision reads as old age, death, or something beyond both.
- Is the "day" when all things change into dearness and forgiveness the far end of a long life, a state after death ("before an eternal, night-like rest"), or a way of seeing available in retrospect at any age? Paragraph 17 leans eschatological and paragraph 14 pulls back to three years; the English has to hold both pulls and cannot afford a word like "heaven" or "in old age" to tip it.
- How far can English go in reproducing the durative, subject-dropping drift of the long sentences before it stops being readable? The margin between keeping her unannounced slide into vision and losing the reader entirely is a judgement that a first-page trial should test rather than a rule that can be set here.
- *Bōya* for a baby introduced as a girl: keep a literal "little boy", soften to a fond "baby/little one", or keep *bōya*? Each costs something — accuracy, warmth, or transparency — and the house should choose deliberately rather than drift.

Voice takes:
(a) Quiet and close: plain diction, long sentences kept long, repetitions unvaried, the vision left dim. (b) Slightly warmer and more idiomatic: domestic scenes eased into natural English rhythm, vision kept plain, at some cost to the circling syntax. (c) More formal and distanced: a cooler, faintly elevated narrative surface matching the Taishō register, risking stiffness in the dialogue.

Crux check — 晩餐 (Shiraki Shizu)

**1. The vision must stay unresolved.** The tasteless potato (p11) slips the mother into a distant stillness (p15–p20) where three years of marriage feel like a lifetime, and life itself is seen from beyond its end — three quiet figures, an endless story containing good and evil, sorrow and joy, all held in なつかしみ, 許し and 安らかさ before a night-like rest. Whether this is death, old age, or exhaustion is never settled; settling it would rewrite the story. *For the English:* do not gloss the vision as heaven, memory, or symbol; keep its vagueness, and repeat the same plain words for 安らかさ／なつかしみ／許し each time rather than varying them elegantly. Let tense and distance drift as hers do.

**2. The hope is the same fact read again, inside the same supper.** What crushes her as an endless life (p13) returns, unchanged, as わづかに三年ばかり (p14) and まだ三年しか (p22, p27) — and becomes grounds for もう少しの間だ, 働きませうね, and rising early tomorrow (p34–p36), framed by the storm unheard (p8), heard (p19), and named again at the close (p38). *For the English:* keep the mirrored phrasing so the reversal is heard, keep the diction plain and repetitive rather than polished, and never sentimentalise the child into a message — the affirmation must stay embodied in spoon-banging, feeding, nursing and clearing the table.

crux.for_the_english: Do not clarify the vision into old age, heaven, a memory, or a symbol with named participants. Keep its vagueness, its level abstract vocabulary, and its repetitions — 安らかさ, なつかしみ/懐しみ, 許し, 静か — returning as the same English words, not elegant synonyms. Let tense and distance drift as hers does; rationalising the syntax into a explained consolation would make the consolation cheaper and more certain than it is.
crux.point: The tasteless potato opens a still, distant vision (p11–p20) in which an only-three-years marriage feels like a whole life, and the whole of life is imagined from beyond itself — three quiet figures telling an endless story in which good, evil, sorrow, anger and joy remain, but are wrapped in なつかしみ, 許し and 安らかさ, on the threshold of a night-like eternal rest. Whether this is death, extreme old age, or a trance of exhaustion is never settled, and that unsettledness is the story.
crux.why: The turn is deliberately slight — a hard, tasteless mouthful, 凍ったかのやうに固くざくざく — and then her heart slips 遠く, repeatedly, until time itself revalues: what oppressed her as endless (p13) becomes, on return, the same fact as hope, わづかに…三年ばかり (p14) and まだ三年しか (p22, p27).

crux.for_the_english: Keep the diction plain, tired and repetitive rather than lyrical in a polished way, and keep the mirrored phrasing of the closing exchanges so the reader hears the same three years first as a lifetime of suffering and then as only three years, with work and tomorrow still ahead. Do not sentimentalise the child into a 'message': the hope has to stay embodied — spoon banging, feeding, nursing, clearing up, the storm heard again at the end (p38) — not stated as uplift.
crux.point: The return from the vision is not an argument but a resumed supper: the second crux is that the story's affirmation is made by the same tired young bodies, cheap food and storm it began with, not by escaping them.
crux.why: The frame is exact: the storm unheard in absorption (p8), heard inside the vision (p19), and named last, 嵐だな (p38); the table cleared, the child asleep at the breast, 起きよう for tomorrow (p36). If the English ennobles the poverty or separates the visionary middle from this domestic plainness, she becomes a poetess commenting on life instead of a exhausted mother whose distance is briefly real and then set down.

payload.english: Outside the door, darkened by now, there was the sound of hard wind and rain — a {t:arashi}.

The parents had gathered around the {t:table} under the dim {t:dento} hanging by the wall of the narrow room, about to take their supper. Father and mother were both still truly young. And the child was a girl, plump and round, just able to stand holding on to the {t:table}.
notes: p2-s3 fixes the child as a girl; Bōya later is kept as the parents' fond address, not a change of sex.

payload.english: Neither the man nor the woman had yet a single wrinkle in the face. But in the hollowed, gentle-looking eyes in the shadow of the man's thick brows there showed a languid colour of tiredness. And in the dark colour of the woman's hair and about her slight shoulders there showed a still more sunken deep tiredness, and a drowsy-like peace.
notes: Keeps peace steady for the yasuraka- family; keeps young-and-already-worn together without ennobling.

hard_spots.why_hard: Long durative sentences bound by soshite/keredomo, likenesses (yō), repetitions of quiet/dear/forgiveness/peace. Advances by returning, not by logic. Child introduced as 女の子 (girl) then called 坊や (bōya, usually boy) by both parents. Fluent fix is to make child a boy. House rule: preserve as parents' fond usage; keep Bōya with note, keep she/her for narrator.
うまうまうまうま with spoon-banging while looking at mother — delight/food word, not standard delicious. Needs consistent child-voice rendering without cute ennoblement.

style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: No surnames or honorifics in text; do not invent. Keep Bōya capitalised as address; keep narrator she/her for mother, she/her for girl child. Name order n/a.

style_sheet.register: Modern plain literary English for narration, no Taishō costume or archaism; dialogue split — his plain rough, her quiet polite-formal — without dialect caricature; baby noise vivid and physical
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Do not carry ruby as parentheses: 卓《テーブル》 → table; 怜悧《れいり》 → shrewd; 微笑《ほゝゑみ》 → smile; 茫然《ぼんやり》 → vaguely/vacantly. No italics for emphasis or thought; italics only for first-use kept Japanese items (Bōya, umma-umma, dobin) where house style requires.
standing_rules: Do not correct girl to boy: girl child addressed as Bōya throughout.
Keep potato adjectives exact and unconnected: frozen-seeming, hard, gritty, flavourless, cold — no diagnosis.
Keep network words invariant: peace/rest, lonely, dearness, forgiveness, far, smile, silent, gaze down/far.
Do not add attributions (she thought, she saw in her mind) where Japanese lets picture be there.
Keep storm first/last lines equally bare; do not moralise ending beyond clear table, sleep, rise early.
Scope: all views, all paragraphs; passage wins over bible — flag conflict plainly.

reading.reading:
The crux is a dilation of time inside an otherwise unremarkable supper, and the translation stands or falls on not explaining it. A young, poor couple are eating with their baby in a narrow room while a storm goes on outside. The mother puts a softly cooked potato in her mouth and finds it hard, gritty, as if frozen, and very bad. Nothing is made of this in dialogue — no complaint, no apology for the cooking — but the tasteless, cold mouthful detaches her. Fatigue, the sadnesses of their married poverty, illness and fear over money, suddenly feel as if they have lasted a lifetime and as if she has grown old; in the same movement she sees, far off and dim, three quiet figures with their heads together telling one endless story in which everything in the world — good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, worry, joy — is being told, while the tellers only smile, unmoving, wrapped in a quiet dearness and forgiveness and a deep peace. She understands, in her own circling terms, that a day will come when everything past will have changed into that dearness and forgiveness, before an eternal, night-like rest. Then the arithmetic returns: it has, in fact, been only three years since the marriage. The rest of the story is her carrying that vision back into the room — twice asked by her husband why she is silent, twice unable to say it — and turning it, without ever reporting it, into a resolve that they will work, that the child will walk, that there is only a little longer to bear. If English makes this a stated epiphany, a vision of heaven, a premonition of death, or a lesson about poverty, it has clarified what Shiraki leaves as a picture seen at the bottom of the eyes; if it makes it merely a tired daydream, it has flattened the one event the story has.

Keep the mechanism plain and physical. The potato passage must stay oddly exact — frozen-seeming, gritty between the front teeth, flavourless, cold, unconnected — because the vision grows out of that sensory wrongness and out of accumulated tiredness, not out of any remark or symbol offered by the narrator. Likewise keep the domestic business exact and unembellished: bowls and the earthen bottle and the aluminium pot cleared under the table out of the baby's reach, the spoon and small plate left, rice steaming from the pot, beef and onion and carrot and potato served from a deep indigo pot, the child banged and fed and finally asleep at the breast. The vision is credible only because the supper is not. Do not let the prose ennoble either side: no lyrical poverty, no squalor either. They are young — the text insists neither face has a wrinkle yet — and already worn, his tiredness in the hollowed, gentle eyes under thick brows, hers in the dark hair and slight shoulders. That double fact, young and exhausted, is what makes her feeling of having aged, and of a life already very long, land.

The sound is long, drifting, durative sentences bound by *soshite* and *keredomo*, full of likenesses — as if a dream, as if a picture, as if far away — and then, against them, short exchanges of dialogue and the child's noise. English will want to rationalise the long sentences into tidy subordination and to vary the words they repeat; resist both. The repetition is the thought. *Shizuka*, *yasuraka*, *samishii/sabishii*, *natsukashii*, *yurushi*, *tooii*, smiling, looking down, looking far away: this small network has to recur in the same English words, so that when "dearness and forgiveness" returns in her silent resolve the reader feels the vision still operating rather than a new sentiment being introduced. In particular do not upgrade *natsukashimi* into full "nostalgia" every time if it makes it sound like a concept; she is feeling a tenderness toward what has not yet even become past. Keep "peace/rest" similarly steady for the *yasuraka-* family, and let the strangeness of feeling it as lonely — a lonely peace, a lonely sigh — survive.

Register is Taishō literary prose in historical kana, but it is not quaint, and the English should not wear period costume. The narration is soft and close, moving without announcement from the room into the mother's inner seeing and back; dropped subjects and unmarked shifts of whose eyes we are through are part of that drift, so repair only what English genuinely cannot carry, and never add attributions ("she thought to herself", "in her mind's eye") where the Japanese simply lets the picture be there. The dialogue is the opposite register: brief, colloquial, his rougher *sō da nā*, *ore-tachi*, her polite feminine forms and her careful *watashitachi wa hatarakimashō ne*. Give her speech a quiet formality and his a plainer roughness without caricature, and keep how little is actually said: he asks twice why she is silent, she answers only that it has really been barely three years, and the most important thing she has to tell him — something large she herself does not understand — is never told. Do not make him obtuse for not understanding, nor her articulate.

Note the frame and do not break it. The storm is announced in the first line, forgotten in the warm noisiness of feeding the child (the text says outright that they do not hear it), heard again by the mother alone at the moment the vision returns, and finally named by the husband, standing still and whispering, after the child is asleep and the room has gone quiet. That progression — unheard, heard inwardly, spoken — is the story's only plot, and the last line must stay as bare as the first. The child is its counterweight throughout: fat, round, precariously standing, banging spoon and plate, crying *umamma* with delight, impossible to keep still for an instant. Keep her vivid and noisy rather than adorable in a generalised way; her present-tense liveliness is what the mother's far-off stillness is seen across, and what the resolve at the end is for. Watch also the small, easy-to-smooth contradiction that the baby is introduced as a girl and then addressed as *bōya*: preserve the address as the parents' fond usage rather than silently correcting the child into a boy.

The likeliest fluent failures, in Berman's terms, are clarification of the vision into old age, death or heaven; destruction of the repeated-word network by elegant variation; rationalisation of the circling sentences in paragraphs 16–20, which think by returning rather than advancing; and ennoblement of the ending into inspiration. The ending is modest: clear the table, sleep, get up early tomorrow. Let it be.
reading.say:
The crux is a dilation of time inside an otherwise unremarkable supper, and the translation stands or falls on not explaining it. A young, poor couple are eating with their baby in a narrow room while a storm goes on outside. The mother puts a softly cooked potato in her mouth and finds it hard, gritty, as if frozen, and very bad. Nothing is made of this in dialogue — no complaint, no apology for the cooking — but the tasteless, cold mouthful detaches her. Fatigue, the sadnesses of their married poverty, illness and fear over money, suddenly feel as if they have lasted a lifetime and as if she has grown old; in the same movement she sees, far off and dim, three quiet figures with their heads together telling one endless story in which everything in the world — good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, worry, joy — is being told, while the tellers only smile, unmoving, wrapped in a quiet dearness and forgiveness and a deep peace. She understands, in her own circling terms, that a day will come when everything past will have changed into that dearness and forgiveness, before an eternal, night-like rest. Then the arithmetic returns: it has, in fact, been only three years since the marriage. The rest of the story is her carrying that vision back into the room — twice asked by her husband why she is silent, twice unable to say it — and turning it, without ever reporting it, into a resolve that they will work, that the child will walk, that there is only a little longer to bear. If English makes this a stated epiphany, a vision of heaven, a premonition of death, or a lesson about poverty, it has clarified what Shiraki leaves as a picture seen at the bottom of the eyes; if it makes it merely a tired daydream, it has flattened the one event the story has.

Keep the mechanism plain and physical. The potato passage must stay oddly exact — frozen-seeming, gritty between the front teeth, flavourless, cold, unconnected — because the vision grows out of that sensory wrongness and out of accumulated tiredness, not out of any remark or symbol offered by the narrator. Likewise keep the domestic business exact and unembellished: bowls and the earthen bottle and the aluminium pot cleared under the table out of the baby's reach, the spoon and small plate left, rice steaming from the pot, beef and onion and carrot and potato served from a deep indigo pot, the child banged and fed and finally asleep at the breast. Do not make him obtuse for not understanding, nor her articulate.

The ending is modest: clear the table, sleep, get up early tomorrow. Let it be.

Open questions:
- Who are the three figures in the vision — the couple and their grown child, the couple grown old with someone else, or no identifiable persons at all? The text says only "three people" in dim light; any identification the English adds, even by pronoun or age, settles what Shiraki leaves unsettled, and the choice will colour whether the vision reads as old age, death, or something beyond both.
- Is the "day" when all things change into dearness and forgiveness the far end of a long life, a state after death ("before an eternal, night-like rest"), or a way of seeing available in retrospect at any age? Paragraph 17 leans eschatological and paragraph 14 pulls back to three years; the English has to hold both pulls and cannot afford a word like "heaven" or "in old age" to tip it.
